note: Volume I, Number 2, and the issue that reads the whole run's first one. Its advertising columns (page 3 columns 5-6, page 4 column 6) carry the SAME advertisements as 1835-06-08 in far better OCR, so five readings the first issue could only bracket are settled here on a second witness: the attorney is R. Stewart, the arms notice is signed J. Green, the painter's shop is on Randolph over Briggs & Humphrey's, the trunk manufactory is a SADDLE and harness one continued by S. B. Cobb, and the unnamed druggist is Frederick Thomas at the drawbridge. Page 2 column 1 carries the land-sale crowd and a population estimate.

Strangers, to the a[mo]unt of some hundreds more, fill our public ho[us]es and str[ee]ts; our wharves are covered with [men], women and children just landed from the vessels, and even some store houses have been thrown open to receive the unsheltered emigrants, who [had else] remained under the open [sk]y upon the wharves. claims.notes: THE TOWN AT THE SCENE DATE, IN THE PAPER'S OWN WORDS, three weeks before it. Two facts this project can use: a population 'supposed to be between 2500 and 3000' — the paper says outright that it is an estimate and not a count, and the confidence must travel with it — and the wharves in the fortnight before the June land sale carrying people, tents and opened store houses. That is a USE claim about the wharf layer, not a geometry one: it says what stood on the wharves, not where the wharves were. OCR is heavy through the passage ('populwon', 'ucenracy', 'coveret!', 'bersts') and every correction above is recognition-class; none of the numbers is touched.

business.name: Russell & Clift, Chicago Book and Stationary Store

claims.notes: THE SAME BOOKSELLER'S ADVERTISEMENT AS 1835-06-08, and the second printing adds hats and shoes to what a Chicago book store also sold. The heading 'Chicago Book and Stationary STORE' is legible in the first issue and lost here, so the business name is carried from that witness; the firm's own abbreviation 'R. & C.' appears in both. Still no address in either printing. The counterfeit warning is quoted because it is the sort of thing that dates a stock: Evans's Hygeian pills were being faked in the west in 1835 and the agent is saying so in his own advertisement.
